evidence: src/domain/entities/Project.ts: `private constructor(readonly id, readonly name)` + `static create` trims the name and throws `ValidationError('Project name must not be empty')`

src/domain/entities/User.ts: `private constructor(readonly id, readonly name)` + `static create` trims the name and throws `ValidationError('User name must not be empty')`. Same shape as Project, but a separate invariant for a different entity

src/domain/entities/Task.ts: `private constructor` + `static create(props: NewTaskProps)`, wraps its title in the `TaskTitle` value object, and `markDone()` throws `ConflictError` if the task is already done
All three entities use the shared `../errors/DomainError` types, so errors are handled the same way across the module
parsedVerdict.reasoning: This passes. All three files deal with one concern, the domain entities. Each one uses the same pattern: a private constructor, a static `create` factory that checks invariants, readonly identity fields, and errors from the shared `DomainError` hierarchy. Each entity keeps its own invariants: Project checks that its name is not empty, User checks that its name is not empty, and Task checks that it cannot be marked done twice. No file bypasses the module's own abstractions. Project and User repeat the same trim-and-check-empty logic. These are separate rules for separate entities, with separate error messages, so this is a small structural likeness rather than one rule copied into two places. A possible future refactor would be to put the name checks into value objects, the way Task already uses `TaskTitle`. Project and User keep the name as a plain string while Task wraps its title in a value object, but that difference is not serious enough to fail the rule.
